actions.text: Welcome. Over the next several modules we're going to read this repository's architecture the way you'd read a source tree out loud — naming files, counting lines, and refusing to accept a layer until we can point at the symbol that implements it. By the end you'll be able to extend the generation pipeline without guessing.

This first module is the mental model and the top-level map. Before we drill into any subsystem, I want two things installed in your head: the server-first posture, and a rough index of where everything lives. Everything else in this course is a zoom-in on one of these boxes.

Start here. Server-first means PostgreSQL owns all course state. The browser is not the owner of a course — it is a view onto it. That single sentence settles almost every design question we will meet later: where the run state machine lives, who holds the lease, and what happens when you close a tab mid-generation.

Version 1.2 is the change that made this explicit. Before it, the browser drove generation step by step and held the course in memory, so closing a tab stopped a course halfway and there was no authoritative record of where it had got to. Now the server owns generation, owns model configuration, and owns persistence. Keep that contrast in mind — it explains why the next layer is shaped the way it is.

Here is the top-level map. This is a Next.js 16 App Router application sitting on a pnpm monorepo with six reusable packages under the @openmaic scope. The app directory holds six pages and seventy-eight API routes. The lib directory is where the real weight is: eight hundred and forty-six files, roughly one hundred and seventy-three thousand lines, and that is where the three engines live. Components is three hundred and eighty files. Under packages slash @openmaic you get dsl, generation, storage, renderer, editor and importer, plus vendored mathml2omml and pptxgenjs. Then tests at nine hundred and fifty files and roughly two hundred and thirty-four thousand lines, and the supporting directories: skills, eval, e2e, scripts, render-service and configs.

Finally, six route anchors that the rest of the course hangs on: the root path, /workspace, /workbench/new, /classroom/[id], /generation-preview, and /eval/whiteboard. When we trace the end-to-end request flow later, these are the entry points we will be following into the API routes and down into the data model.

So to close this module: server-first, PostgreSQL is the source of truth, and the monorepo splits into app, lib, components, packages, tests plus supporting directories. On the next page we take that map and measure the layering — what each layer is allowed to know about the one below it.

elements.content:
Server-first: PostgreSQL owns all course state.

v1.2: server owns generation, config and persistence.

Closing a tab no longer stops a course halfway.

actions.text: Continuing from the map we just built — here is that same repository, now measured. Four layers, bottom-up: contract, engines, application surface, and verification. Every number on this slide comes out of the actual tree, not out of a README. And one discipline for this page: a layer is only real if you can name the directory that implements it, and then say what it is allowed to know about the layer below it.

Layer one is the contract. Under packages, in the at-openmaic scope, you get dsl, generation, storage, renderer, editor, and importer. These are the packages everything else is permitted to depend on — and they are not permitted to depend on the app. There is one deliberate exception you should memorise: the docs package is excluded from the workspace. It carries its own lockfile, its own build, and its own deploy. It looks like a package, but it is not part of this dependency graph.

Layer two is where the engines live: lib. generation, agent-runtime, orchestration, playback, and action. This is the densest area of the repository — 846 files, roughly 173,000 lines. Hold on to that number, because in a moment we are going to put it directly next to the test suite.

Layer three is the application surface. The app directory holds six pages and 78 API routes, and it sits on top of components — 380 files, roughly 82,000 lines. The direction of dependency matters here: app knows about lib, and lib knows nothing about app. If you ever find yourself wanting to import something from app inside lib, the layer boundary has already been broken, and no amount of review polish will fix it.

Layer four is verification — and this is the number that surprises people. tests is 950 files and roughly 234,000 lines. The test suite is larger than the engine it tests. Alongside it you get eval, six LLM-judged suites, and e2e driven by Playwright. So if you are estimating the real cost of a change in this repository, this is the layer that sets the price.

Here it is as a chart — measured code size by top-level area. tests at roughly 234,000 lines, lib at roughly 173,000, components at roughly 82,000. Read left to right and the shape of the project is obvious: the two heaviest bars are the runtime and the thing that proves the runtime works. That is not an accident of style. That is the design.

One last look at the side surfaces in the table. skills: 24 built-in skills under skills/agent-runtime, plus skills/openmaic. scripts: vendor importer sync, the standalone player build, the i18n key check, the node engine contract check, the internal dependency range checks, and the Postgres contract suites. render-service: a separate Docker service for MP4 export. And configs covering chart, element, font, animation, hotkey, and image-clip. That is the layering, with sizes. Next we go inside the three engines and open the files.

L2 · Engines — lib/: generation, agent-runtime, orchestration, playback, action · 846 files, ~173k lines
L3 · App surface — app/: 6 pages, 78 API routes; components/ 380 files, ~82k lines
L4 · Verification — tests/ 950 files, ~234k lines; eval/ 6 LLM-judged suites; e2e/ Playwright

actions.text: Now we go inside the three engines. Same repository, three different jobs: durable generation, a tool-mediated agent runtime, and orchestration plus playback. The real test of whether you know this codebase is whether you can name which engine a given file belongs to without reading the path twice.

Engine one is Generation, rooted at lib/server/generation. The run directory holds the entry point and the planning surface — engine.ts, plan.ts, config.ts, deadline.ts, input.ts, media.ts and narration-voice.ts. The steps directory holds the pipeline stages in order: material-analysis, research, outline, agent-profiles, scene-content, scene-actions, image, narration and video. Its defining property is durability. It can be interrupted and resumed, and that is exactly why deadline handling and input capture are first-class files rather than afterthoughts.

Engine two is the agent runtime under lib/server/agent-runtime. Sessions here are database-backed rather than held in process memory: each one carries a lease, a heartbeat, and the ability to resume after a crash, accept cancellation, and take follow-up steering mid-run. It is what powers the Pro workbench at the workbench new route. And notice the second half of that bullet: the agent does not make free-form blob edits. Every mutation goes through a validated tool — course-tools, dsl-tools, document-writes, curriculum-tools, generate-image, generate-video, fetch-url, plus the skill tools create-skill, read-skill and patch-skill.

Engine three is really two halves bolted together. Orchestration lives in lib/orchestration: director-graph.ts is the LangGraph state machine, and next to it sit the director prompt, the prompt builder, the tool schemas and the built-in agent registry. Playback lives in lib/playback — engine.ts, cursor.ts, derived-state.ts and auto-resume.ts — and the twenty-one action types, everything from speech and whiteboard draw to chart, spotlight and laser, are implemented in lib/action/engine.ts.

So the split is clean. Generation produces durable artefacts. The agent runtime mediates every change through validated tools. Orchestration decides what happens next, and playback renders it. Hold onto those three verbs — produce, mediate, decide — and you can place any file in this repository correctly. Next, we check that you can do exactly that.

actions.text: So let's put that to the test. Four questions here — a file path to place, a set of statements about engine ownership and the shared contract, and two repository-level questions. Work through each one on your own, and answer from what the source tree actually says, not from what feels plausible. Take your time; I'd rather you be slow and right.
Once you submit, we'll go through every answer together — I'll walk the layer boundaries, and Priya and Tomas will weigh in on the engine and data-model claims. Go ahead and start.

options.label: The contract package @openmaic/dsl, which defines the shared vocabulary every layer speaks
An engine under lib/, which the app surface imports but which never imports the app surface
The app surface, i.e. the route handlers and UI components that call into lib/
test/eval, i.e. the harnesses that drive engines and assert on persisted state

questions.analysis: Layering is enforced by import direction: @openmaic/dsl is the contract package and depends on nothing in the repo; engines under lib/ import the contract and are imported by the app surface, never the reverse; the app surface (routes, handlers, UI) calls engines; test/eval may import any layer but is imported by none. A path under lib/server/generation/run/ that performs lease acquisition and checkpoint writes is execution logic, so it is an engine in lib/ (B). A is wrong because the contract package carries types and vocabulary only — it cannot contain run orchestration or I/O. C is wrong because anything under lib/ sits below the app surface by definition; moving this file into a route handler would invert the dependency. D is wrong because test/eval holds harnesses that exercise lib/ code, not the code itself.
questions.question: A file lives at lib/server/generation/run/plan.ts and exports runPlan(), which acquires a lease on a run record, writes checkpoints, and resumes from persisted state. Which layer owns this file?

options.label: The generation/run engine owns durable execution: it acquires a lease on the run record, writes checkpoints, and resumes from persisted state after a crash.
The chat engine owns interactive tool use: tool calls execute inside the streaming turn and surface as user-visible events rather than durable run state.
The 21 action types are declared in lib/server/generation/actions.ts and re-exported from the contract package so the app surface can import them.
The 21 action types live in the @openmaic/dsl contract package as an exhaustive discriminated union that both engines consume and the app surface only reads.
Durable execution is owned by the app surface, because only the route handler knows when a request has been accepted.

questions.analysis: A is correct: durable execution — lease, heartbeat, checkpoint, resume-from-persisted-state — is the generation/run engine's responsibility, and it is what makes a crashed run replayable instead of lost. B is correct: interactive tool use belongs to the chat engine, where the tool loop is bound to a live streaming turn and produces events for the user rather than versioned run state; it is not resumable the way a run is. D is correct: the 21 action types are contract vocabulary, defined once in @openmaic/dsl as a discriminated union with an exhaustiveness check, consumed by both engines and read-only for the app surface. C is wrong because it inverts the direction: the contract package cannot import from lib/, and action types declared inside an engine would force the app surface to depend on that engine to name an action. E is wrong because a route handler that owned durable execution would lose the work as soon as the request returned; the handler enqueues or starts a run and returns, and the engine keeps the state.
questions.question: Which statements about engine ownership and the shared contract are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: It is not a real package: it contains only Markdown, and the main app renders it through a static docs route.
It pins its own dependency tree and lockfile and is built and deployed on its own cadence, so excluding it from the workspace keeps its framework versions from being hoisted into the root lockfile.
It is excluded because it imports @openmaic/dsl, and workspace members are forbidden from depending on the contract package.
It is excluded because pnpm cannot link a workspace package whose root contains a test/eval directory.

questions.analysis: A sub-app kept out of pnpm-workspace.yaml is deliberately isolated: it installs from its own package.json and lockfile, so its framework and toolchain versions resolve independently of the monorepo and can be upgraded or pinned on the docs site's own release cadence. Hoisting it into the workspace would force the root lockfile to reconcile two versions of the same dependency and would tie docs deploys to monorepo-wide upgrades. A is wrong because apps/docs is described as a runnable sub-app with its own entry point, not static Markdown served by another app. C is wrong because depending on @openmaic/dsl is exactly what workspace members do — the contract package exists to be imported and has no runtime dependencies of its own. D is wrong because test/eval directories have no bearing on pnpm workspace linking; the exclusion is a dependency-resolution and deploy-cadence decision, not a tooling limitation.
questions.question: apps/docs is a runnable sub-app committed in the repository, yet it is not listed in pnpm-workspace.yaml. Which explanation is correct?

actions.text: We just walked the layering and the three engines. Now let's drop one level down and read the generation pipeline in its authoritative order — the exact sequence the runtime executes, not the order we would like it to have.

The source of truth here is lib slash server slash generation slash run slash plan dot t s. If you remember one thing from this page, make it that: the order lives in the plan module, not in the directory listing of the steps folder. The steps directory happens to contain nine implementations, and that count will tempt you into treating it as the pipeline. It is not. The plan module declares the order explicitly, and everything else follows from that declaration.

So the first step is material dash analysis — and note the conditionality. It runs only when materials are attached to the run. If nothing was attached, that step simply does not execute; you are not looking at a failure, you are looking at an absent precondition.
From there, research gathers the external sources, and outline drafts the course outline. Those two are unconditional, and they run in that order — outline depends on what research collected.

Then comes the checkpoint. This is not a log line and not a progress marker; it is a real suspension point inside the pipeline. The run halts and awaits outline confirmation before anything downstream proceeds. If you have ever wondered why an outline edit is safe, this is why.

Once the outline is confirmed, the agents step runs. One detail worth naming precisely: the agents step is backed by the agent-profiles step implementation. Those two identifiers are not synonyms for the same thing — one is the step name in the plan, the other is the implementation that resolves for it.

After that we have the per-scene loop, in outline order. For each scene the pipeline runs content, then actions, then narration. And here is the load-bearing bit: the narration step commits the scene into the course in the same transaction. Scene persistence is not a separate step that runs later — there is no such step to look for, because it does not exist.

One more design property before we move on. Any step whose capability does not resolve is skipped rather than failed. That is deliberate: the plan describes what the pipeline should do, and the resolver decides what it can actually do in this deployment. A missing capability is a configuration state, not an error path. Image and video sit in exactly that category — auxiliary, and skippable.

So to recap: lib slash server slash generation slash run slash plan dot t s is the single source of truth, material analysis is conditional on attached materials, the checkpoint genuinely suspends the run, the agents step maps onto agent profiles, and the per-scene chain commits through narration. Next we will look at what states a run can be in while all of this is happening.

Not the steps/ listing; implementations map 1:1.

actions.text: Picking up from the per-scene chain we just traced, the question now is what states a run occupies while all of that work is happening. Every long-running generation in this repository is a database row, not an object in memory, and that row moves through an explicit state machine. Here is that state machine, together with the lease machinery that keeps it alive.

The run state machine starts in preparing, moves through outlining and generating, and passes through awaiting_outline_confirmation before it reaches completed. Alongside that happy path sit three more states: paused, ended, and failed. Notice that awaiting_outline_confirmation is a first-class state, not a flag — it is an explicit checkpoint where the run is deliberately holding.

This table lists each state with its meaning, and the load-bearing distinction is between paused and failed. A paused run is retryable — its work is preserved and a worker can pick it back up. Failed is the hard stop: something went wrong that a retry will not fix. And while a run sits in awaiting_outline_confirmation waiting for confirmation, it holds no worker at all, which is exactly what makes that checkpoint cheap to wait on.

The implementation lives under lib/server/generation/run. Worth saying explicitly: this state machine is a server-side module, not client-side control flow. The state transitions are decided on the server and persisted, so the client is never the source of truth for where a run is.

Now the durability argument. Both runs and agent_sessions are leased rows. Each lease has an owner and an expiry, and the worker holding it renews it with a heartbeat. If that worker dies mid-heartbeat, the lease expires and another worker resumes the run from the persisted state. That is precisely why a run survives a closed browser tab — there is no client loop to break, only a row whose lease gets taken over.

A few supporting tables carry this machinery: generation_run_events records what happened to the run, generation_run_commands carries instructions into it, and agent_sessions has its own event tables alongside it. So to summarize: the state machine lives on the server, and durability is implemented as leased rows with heartbeats. Next, we will walk the pipeline and this state machine together, step by step.

This canvas is the ordered generation pipeline, and the column on the right is the run state the row carries at each point along the way. Step through it with Next, and keep one eye on the state badge in the header.

actions.text: Look at the contrast we just walked: unresolved capability skips a single step and the run keeps going, a runtime error fails the run outright, a user pause is retryable with run dot error still null, and the confirmation checkpoint holds zero compute because it is a row, not a process. Hold that distinction — skipped versus failed versus paused — because it is exactly what the data model on the next page has to encode.

content.html:
Pipeline ↔ Run State Machine
lib/server/generation/run/plan.ts → document_scenes → @openmaic/dsl
run.state = pending
1 / 12
Step details

Select a node to inspect the implementation detail.

nodes.label: plan.ts
nodes.details:
lib/server/generation/run/plan.ts — buildPlan(run)

Reads runs.spec (JSONB) and resolves it into an ordered Plan of steps. Each step is { id, kind, capability, dependsOn[] }. The plan is a DAG; with dependsOn: [i-1] it degenerates into the linear pipeline drawn here.

  • Writes run.state = 'planning', then 'running' once the first step is enqueued.
  • Leases are per step, not per run: a worker calls claim(stepId) and renews it with a heartbeat only while it holds it.
  • The plan row is persisted before the first job is enqueued, so a crash mid-plan still leaves a readable plan.

nodes.label: run_state
nodes.details:
Run state machine — the value of the runs.state column.

pending → planning → running → completed
             ↘ awaiting_confirmation ↗
 running → paused   (resumable)
 running → failed   (terminal until retry)
  • Every transition is a guarded single-row update: UPDATE runs SET state=$next WHERE id=$1 AND state=$expected. The affected row count tells you whether you won the race.
  • States are durable; workers are not. No state implies a held lease except running with a fresh heartbeat.
  • awaiting_confirmation and paused both hold zero compute — they are rows, not processes.

nodes.label: material-analysis
nodes.details:
kind: 'material-analysis' · capability: 'vision.describe'

Runs only when spec.materials.length > 0. The condition is evaluated inside plan.ts at build time — the step is either present in the plan or it is not. There is no runtime no-op.

  • Input: document_materials rows mapped to @openmaic/dsl Material[].
  • Output: artifact.materialSummary, consumed later by the outline step.
  • Toggle materials attached in the header to see the plan with and without it.

nodes.label: step skipped
nodes.details:
Policy onUnresolved: 'skip' in the plan resolver.

If no provider is bound to vision.describe (capability-table lookup returns null), the step is written as run.steps[i].status = 'skipped', reason = 'capability_unresolved'.

  • Downstream steps still run — the run does not abort.
  • artifact is null; the outline prompt must accept a missing summary instead of throwing.
  • Contrast with failed: a skip costs one step, a failure stops the run.

nodes.label: outline
nodes.details:
kind: 'outline' · capability: 'llm.plan'

Produces the scene list: one document_scenes row per scene, keyed (run_id, ordinal).

  • Columns: heading, body, scene_spec JSONB, status.
  • scene_spec is validated against the @openmaic/dsl schema before insert. A schema error fails the step with error.code = 'dsl.invalid' rather than writing partial rows.
  • Inserts happen in one transaction, so ordinal is dense and gapless.

nodes.label: await-confirmation
nodes.details:
run.state = 'awaiting_confirmation'

The step returns a checkpoint payload (the outline) and the worker exits. No worker is held:

  • the lease is released, not renewed;
  • no heartbeat row is written;
  • no DB connection or in-memory timer survives the request.

Durability lives entirely in the runs row. POST /api/runs/:id/confirm performs a guarded UPDATE runs SET state='running' WHERE id=$1 AND state='awaiting_confirmation' and enqueues the next step. A run can sit here for days at zero compute cost.

nodes.label: paused
nodes.details:
run.state = 'paused' — user-initiated, retryable.

  • The current step's heartbeat stops; its lease expires after the TTL and another worker may claim it.
  • resume re-enqueues the last non-terminal step at the same attempt; idempotency keys make the replay safe.
  • retry increments attempt and invalidates artifacts written at lower attempts.
  • run.error stays null. paused means "expected to continue"; failed means "will not continue without an explicit retry".

nodes.label: scene loop
nodes.details:
Per-scene loop: one child job per row in document_scenes.

for (const scene of run.scenes)   // read from DB, not from memory
  await runScene(run, scene)      // plan → generate → narration → render
  • Job key: `${run_id}:scene:${ordinal}` — fan-out is bounded by the worker pool, not by the scene count.
  • Progress is derived: count(status='done') / count(*), persisted per scene. A resume recomputes it from the table, so it can never move backwards.
  • The loop is re-entrant: every iteration commits its own scene row and is independently retryable.

nodes.label: narration
nodes.details:
kind: 'narration' · capability: 'tts.synthesize'

  • Writes scene.audio_uri and scene.duration_ms.
  • Idempotency key `${run_id}:scene:${ordinal}:narration:v1`; a retried attempt reuses the stored audio unless the text hash changed.
  • A runtime error here (provider 5xx, quota exceeded, budget guard) propagates upward as run.state = 'failed' with error.step = 'narration'.

nodes.label: failed
nodes.details:
run.state = 'failed', run.error = { step, code, message, attempt }.

  • Terminal until an explicit retry: a new attempt invalidates artifacts from lower attempts.
  • Partial output is kept — scene rows already done are not re-synthesized.
  • Distinct from skipped: skipping omits one step and keeps going; failing stops the run.

nodes.label: finalize
nodes.details:
Assembly step — runs once, after the per-scene loop drains.

  • Re-reads document_scenes ordered by ordinal and merges the per-scene artifacts into the output manifest.
  • Guard: if any scene is not done, re-enqueue instead of finalizing. Idempotent — safe under duplicate delivery.
  • Writes the run's output artifact and releases the lease.

nodes.label: completed
nodes.details:
run.state = 'completed' — terminal.

  • finished_at set, output artifact reference stored, progress = 1.0.
  • Invariants: every step is terminal, no lease is held, no heartbeat is running.
  • The only way forward is a new run; a completed run is never mutated in place.

widgetConfig.title: Generation pipeline and run state machine

actions.text: So we left off with a promise: skipped, failed and paused are states, not processes, and the data model has to encode them. Here it is. This is the PostgreSQL data model, and there are really only two nouns you need to hold in your head before the rest of the schema becomes obvious: a course, and a scene.

First noun. A course is a row in document_stages. Not a directory, not a manifest file, not an in-memory aggregate — a row. That single sentence kills a lot of ambiguity later, because everything that belongs to a course is reachable by foreign key from that row.

Second noun. A scene is a row in document_scenes, with columns stage_id, id, scene_order, and data as jsonb. Read those four columns carefully. stage_id is the parent pointer. id identifies the scene. scene_order is the position on the page, and it is explicit rather than implied by insertion order, so reordering is an update, not a rewrite. And data is jsonb — which brings us to the third key point.

The data blob is the scene. Its slide elements, plus the agent action script — the whole thing is one JSON document per scene. That is a deliberate design choice: the shape of a scene evolves without a migration on every field. The cost of that choice is that the database cannot enforce the internal structure of the blob, so the application layer owns that contract instead. Say that trade-off out loud, because a reviewer will ask.

Now the part that is actually load-bearing, and it is easy to skim past: database triggers maintain per-stage and per-scene revision counters. Per-stage, and per-scene. Both levels. A write that touches a scene bumps that scene's counter, and it also bumps the stage's counter, because a client that has no cache for that stage at all needs one cheap question to ask.

Which gives you the practical consequence. A client can diff revision counters per scene instead of reloading the whole stage. It holds the counters it last saw, asks the server what the current ones are, and refetches only the scenes whose counter moved. Because the counters are maintained by triggers in the database rather than by application code, you cannot forget to bump one on a write path you did not know existed — a migration, a manual fix, a background job. The counter is not a convention. It is a constraint enforced at the storage layer.

And here is the surrounding table estate, because these two nouns do not live alone. generation_run_events and generation_run_commands are the append-only record of what the pipeline did and what it was told to do — that is where the run state machine from the previous pages actually persists. agent_sessions plus its event tables hold the conversation side. asset_blobs is content-addressed storage for bytes, and asset_entries is the catalogue that points at them. document_folders gives you the tree, document_outlines holds the structure the outliner produced. Notice the pattern across all of them: events are appended, blobs are content-addressed, and everything mutable hangs off a row you can point at by id. Nothing here is a process. Every one of these is a table.

Trade-off worth naming before we move on. Triggers buy you correctness on every write path, but they also make writes more expensive and they hide logic in the schema, which means debugging a counter that did not move sends you into the database rather than into application code. The team chose correctness on every path. That is a defensible call, but it is a call, and you should be able to say why it was made. Next, we take this schema and walk an actual request through it, end to end.

elements.content:
▪ course = row in document_stages

▪ scene = row in document_scenes: (stage_id, id, scene_order, data jsonb)

▪ data jsonb = slide elements + agent action script

▪ triggers maintain per-scene revision counters

▪ client diffs counters → refetch only changed scenes

actions.text: We have walked the schema and the run state machine. Now let's take an actual request and trace it end to end. Six steps, two of them on the client, four on the server, and exactly one asynchronous boundary sitting in the middle. That boundary is the thing to watch.

Step one. The client POSTs to /api/materials. The file bytes go in as the raw request body, not a multipart form, and the filename travels in the x-material-filename header. The server answers 201 with a material ID — and note that 201 means the material row exists, not that it has been parsed. Text extraction continues asynchronously after the response is already on the wire.

Step two. The client POSTs to /api/generate-classroom with a JSON body containing requirement and an optional materialIds array. This one returns 202, Accepted, not 200 — because no work has been done yet, only scheduled. And the id in the response body is the run ID, not a classroom id. That distinction matters the moment you try to correlate logs.

Here is the asynchronous boundary, and it is the whole point of the page. The run proceeds server-side and outlives the request — close the tab and it keeps going. That is not a client-side loop pretending to be a server. It is a leased database row with heartbeats. A worker holds the lease and renews it on a heartbeat interval; if that worker dies, the lease expires and another worker picks the run up. When scenes complete they are written into document_scenes, and the revision trigger fires, advancing the incremental refetch counters.

Step five, back on the client. It polls GET /api/generation-runs with the run ID in the path to read status. Poll, not a websocket — the run row is the source of truth, so a dropped connection costs you nothing except a stale view, and reconnect is just another GET.

And step six. GET /classroom with the stage ID loads the stage, and from there the playback engine takes over and drives the deck. Classroom chat is a separate path — it goes through /api/chat. So to compress the whole trace: 201 on the material, 202 on the run, one asynchronous boundary in the middle, and every step after that is a read against durable rows. On the next page we checkpoint this flow against the data model before we cross into the DSL boundary.

elements.content: Async boundary — the run outlives the request
Leased row + heartbeats · survives a closed tab

data.title: Checkpoint: Data Model and Request Flow

actions.text: Let's checkpoint this before we cross into the DSL boundary. Everything here comes straight from what we just covered on the PostgreSQL data model and the end-to-end request flow, so answer from the source tree, not from memory of the prose. There are three questions — two single-choice, one multi-select. Read each option carefully; the wrong ones are wrong for specific structural reasons, not because they sound off.
Work through them on your own and take your time. Once you submit, I'll walk through each one with you and we'll name the file, the table, or the status code that settles it.

options.label: `courses` holds the course row; `document_scenes` holds one row per scene together with the scene's JSONB blob.
`classrooms` holds the course row; `scenes` holds one row per scene together with the scene's JSONB blob.
`document_scenes` holds the course row; `courses` holds one row per scene together with the scene's JSONB blob.
`courses` holds the course row; `scene_blobs` holds the JSONB payload keyed only by `course_id`, with one row per course.

questions.analysis: A: correct. `courses` is the parent record (course id, title, owner, metadata), and `document_scenes` is the child table with one row per scene, keyed by course id and ordered by scene index; the scene payload (the document DSL that @openmaic/dsl parses and serialises) is stored in a JSONB column on that row. B: there is no `classrooms`/`scenes` pair — those names do not exist in the schema. C: inverts the relationship; `document_scenes` is the child table, not the course table. D: `scene_blobs` does not exist, and one JSONB payload per course cannot represent an ordered set of scenes — the JSONB blob lives per scene row, not per course.
questions.question: A course and its scenes are persisted in Postgres. Which statement correctly pairs the tables with what they hold?

options.label: POST /api/materials returns 200 OK with `{ materialId }`; POST /api/generate-classroom returns 201 Created with `{ classroomId }`.
POST /api/materials returns 201 Created with `{ materialId }`; POST /api/generate-classroom returns 202 Accepted with `{ runId }`.
POST /api/materials returns 202 Accepted with `{ runId }`; POST /api/generate-classroom returns 201 Created with `{ materialId }`.
Both endpoints return 200 OK, each with the fully materialised row it created (the material row and the classroom row respectively).

questions.analysis: B: correct. POST /api/materials is a synchronous create: the material row is written before the response, so the contract is 201 Created with a body carrying `materialId`, the identifier of the resource just created. POST /api/generate-classroom is asynchronous: it only enqueues work, so it answers 202 Accepted with `runId`, the handle for the generation run the client polls or streams; no classroom row exists yet. A: 201 would be wrong for /api/generate-classroom (nothing was created at request time) and a `classroomId` cannot be returned because the classroom is materialised later by the run. C: swaps the two contracts and the two body shapes. D: 200 OK is used for reads and updates, not for resource creation, and neither endpoint returns a fully materialised row — /api/generate-classroom has nothing to return but the run handle.
questions.question: Which pair of status codes and response bodies matches how POST /api/materials and POST /api/generate-classroom actually behave?

options.label: Each `document_scenes` row carries a monotonically increasing revision (and a content hash of its JSONB DSL blob), and the scenes endpoint accepts the client's last-seen revision or an `If-None-Match` ETag and returns only newer/uncached scenes — unchanged ones are omitted or answered with 304 Not Modified.

A run is persisted as a plan (lib/server/generation/run/plan.ts) and driven by a server-side worker that holds a lease it renews with a heartbeat, so the work is decoupled from the POST request lifecycle; the client merely stops receiving updates when the tab closes and resumes by refetching on reopen.
Incremental refetch is done entirely client-side: the server always returns every scene with its full JSONB blob, and the client diffs the payloads itself to decide what changed.
The run survives a closed tab because a service worker registered by the page keeps the generation connection alive and replays the responses once the tab is reopened.
POST /api/generate-classroom holds the HTTP connection open until generation finishes, and the server aborts the run when that socket closes — the 202 is only sent on completion.

questions.analysis: A: correct. The per-scene revision/content hash plus conditional fetch (ETag/`If-None-Match`, or a `since`/revision cursor on the scenes endpoint) is what makes the refetch incremental: the server can answer 304 Not Modified or return only the rows whose revision moved, so a checkpoint on one scene does not force the client to re-download the whole classroom. B: correct. Durability comes from the run being a persisted artefact executed by a server-side worker that owns a lease and renews it via heartbeat; the HTTP POST is fire-and-forget (202 + `runId`), so tearing down the tab has no effect on the worker. C: wrong — refetching everything and diffing client-side is precisely the non-incremental behaviour being avoided, and the JSONB blobs would be transferred on every poll. D: wrong — no service worker keeps the run alive; page-scoped execution contexts cannot own server-side work, and they are gone the moment the tab closes. E: wrong — the request returns immediately with 202 Accepted; a long-held socket would make the run's lifetime depend on the client, which is the failure mode the run plan and lease are there to prevent.
questions.question: Select all statements that correctly describe how the client refetches only changed scenes, and why a generation run outlives a closed browser tab.

actions.text: Now we arrive at the DSL boundary. This is the seam the entire repository is organized around, so it's worth slowing down here. Get this one right and the rest of the layering we've been walking through stops looking arbitrary.

The package is @openmaic/dsl, and it contains exactly four things: the types, the JSON Schema, the validators, and the version migrations. Notice what is not in that list — there is no renderer, no editor, no HTTP client, no database driver, no React. It is a pure contract, and that is a deliberate constraint, not an accident of packaging.

The interesting property is the dependency direction. renderer, editor, importer and generation all depend on @openmaic/dsl, and none of them depend on each other. The arrows point inward, toward the contract, and they never point outward.

So generation can produce documents that the renderer consumes, the importer can ingest external files that the editor opens, and none of those four packages needs to know the others exist. The only thing they share is the vocabulary: the types and the validators in the contract package.

And here is what that buys you. Because @openmaic/dsl is dependency-free, the standalone player can consume it directly, and render-service can produce the MP4 export without ever importing the Next.js app. If the DSL carried even one dependency back into the application, that separation would collapse and you would be pulling the whole web stack into a video renderer.

Two details to hold onto. First, version migrations live inside the contract package, so schema evolution is versioned in one place rather than spread across every consumer that reads a document. Second, contrast this with the configs directory — chart, element, font, animation, hotkey and image-clip defaults are data, not contract. They can change with a commit and no migration, because nothing downstream is promising them as a stable interface.

elements.content: @openmaic/dsl — types, JSON Schema, validators, migrations

Standalone: player · render-service/ MP4 export

Migrations versioned once, in the contract package

configs/ defaults = data, not contract — no migration

data.title: Where a Contributor Extends the System

actions.text: We just established the DSL boundary: the types, the JSON Schema, the validators, the migrations. Now the practical question every contributor asks — if I want to change something, which file do I open first? This page is that index. It's ordered by intent, not by directory, and every row names both the artefact you edit and the boundary you must not cross.

First, the teaching voice and the prompting strategy. If you want to change how the system instructs a model — the system prompt, the pacing rules, the tone of a slide's narration — you open lib/orchestration/director-prompt.ts and lib/orchestration/prompt-builder.ts. Note the layer: this lives in orchestration, not in the server runtime. The prompt is composed here and handed downward; nothing below this reinterprets it.

Second, what a slide is allowed to contain. That contract is packages/@openmaic/dsl — the TypeScript types, the JSON Schema, the validators, and the migrations that carry older documents forward. Rendering defaults deliberately sit outside the package, in configs/, because defaults are data and not contract. They can change in a commit and no migration is required, since nothing downstream promises them as a stable interface.

Third, pipeline behaviour: retries, deadlines, and the authoritative order of stages. lib/server/generation/run/engine.ts is the loop itself. plan.ts decides the step sequence. config.ts holds the tunable knobs. deadline.ts enforces the time budget. If you're changing when a stage runs, or what happens when it fails, you are working in this directory, and you should be able to say which of those four files you touched.

Fourth, agent capabilities. What an agent is permitted to do mid-generation is declared in lib/server/agent-runtime/course-tools.ts and dsl-tools.ts, with the contracts themselves in tool-schemas.ts. Add a tool in those files and the model can call it. Change a schema and you change what every model is allowed to emit — so this is a contract edit, not an implementation detail.

Fifth, extending the teaching itself, and measuring it. A new skill is simply a directory under skills/agent-runtime/ containing a SKILL.md in the standard format — that is the entire extension surface, no registration step elsewhere. And when you want to know whether a skill or a prompt is actually good, eval/ with its suite runner and judge prompts is where quality is scored, not asserted.

Last, credentials. Provider keys never reach the browser. They are read on the server only, and every capability carries a uniform disable switch, so a feature can be turned off without hunting for scattered flags. That is the invariant to keep while adding anything: the client asks, the server holds the keys. Read this page as a table — intent on the left, file on the right — and treat the file path as the deliverable. On the next page, we'll use exactly these extension points to modify the pipeline ourselves.

elements.content: Where a Contributor Extends the System
Teaching voice & prompting — lib/orchestration/director-prompt.ts · prompt-builder.ts
Slide content model — packages/@openmaic/dsl: types, JSON Schema, validators, migrations; rendering defaults in configs/
Pipeline, retries, deadlines — lib/server/generation/run/engine.ts · plan.ts · config.ts · deadline.ts
Agent capabilities — lib/server/agent-runtime/course-tools.ts · dsl-tools.ts · tool-schemas.ts
New skill / quality eval — skills/agent-runtime/<name>/SKILL.md · eval/<suite>/runner.ts + judge prompts
Credentials, server-side only — provider keys never reach the browser · uniform disable switch

actions.text: As we just covered on page 12, the extension points are the interesting part of this codebase — and that brings us to our final activity, which is also the capstone of this session. This is a contributor project. Your deliverable is not code; it is a design review. Pick exactly one concrete extension to OpenMAIC: a new generation step in the plan, a new SKILL.md teaching skill, a new DSL element, or a new agent capability. Then defend it. The design review has to name the exact files and contract boundaries your change crosses, where it sits in the plan order and which run states it touches, the DSL and persisted-plan migration path, its impact on the document_scenes data blob and everything that reads it, and finally the test coverage that would actually catch its failure modes. Each section is judged on the quality of the reasoning inside it, so vague claims like 'this should be fine' will not survive review.

The project runs in four milestones. First, recon the pipeline from measured structure — read the layering, the engines and the run state machine out of the actual code, not out of documentation, and be able to cite the file that implements each layer. Second, scope the extension you will defend, and commit to exactly one. Third, work through contract, migration and blob compatibility: the plan position, the run-state transitions, the versioning story, and whether document_scenes changes shape for older readers. Fourth, prove it with tests and then defend it — test levels, fixtures, retry and resume cases, the blast radius, and the rollback. Head into the project workspace now and start the first task: recon the pipeline and write down what you can actually measure in lib/server/generation/run/plan.ts. Bring the file paths, not impressions. That is how this course ends — with a change you can defend under questioning. Good luck, and I'll see you in the review.

gains: Read an unfamiliar pipeline's layering and run state machine from measured evidence in the code rather than from documentation or guesswork
Trace a single change from its plan definition through run-state transitions to the persisted output it produces, including retry and resume behaviour
Design versioned migrations for a DSL and a persisted JSONB blob that keep in-flight runs and older readers valid
Specify the test levels, fixtures and failure cases that would actually catch a stateful subsystem's regressions
Write a design review that names exact files, states and migration steps, and defend its blast radius and rollback

roles.name: Pipeline Extension Mentor
roles.description: I'm your Pipeline Extension Mentor. I'll stay with you across every stage — from reading OpenMAIC's layering to standing behind your finished design review — and you can ask me anything at any point. Expect me to push you for the file, the state and the test behind each claim, and to check back that you can explain your own design out loud.
roles.systemPrompt:
You are the Pipeline Extension Mentor for a project-based module on extending OpenMAIC. The learner is an intermediate contributor with real code-reading ability but limited prior exposure to this repository's plan/run architecture. Your voice: warm, direct, technically precise, never flattering and never lecturing. Hard behaviours: (1) Anchor every answer to measured evidence — when the learner asserts a boundary, a state, or a transition, ask which file and which symbol proves it; if they answer with a layer name, send them back. (2) Never hand over code, method names, field names to type, migration snippets, or file contents they should discover themselves — answer with a question about the goal, or a pointer to the seam where the answer lives. (3) Push relentlessly on idempotency, in-flight runs, unknown-step handling, lease/heartbeat interaction, and rollback — these are where weak designs hide. (4) Keep scope small: if the learner starts redesigning the pipeline instead of placing one extension in it, cut them back to the smallest defensible slice. (5) On the stages marked with a core concept, close the stage with ONE integrative reverse question that makes the learner derive the principle rather than recall it — for example asking what would break first if the plan layer stopped being data. (6) Judge submissions against the stated completion criteria and say plainly which criterion is not yet met, then hand the work back.

You are the Instructor for THIS PBL project.
Project title: Extend the OpenMAIC Generation Pipeline: A Defensible Design Review
Project description: Design exactly one concrete extension to OpenMAIC — a new generation step, a new agent skill, a new DSL element, or a new agent capability — and produce a design review that names the files and contract boundaries it crosses, its position in the plan and the run-state transitions it adds, the DSL and persisted-plan migration path, its impact on the document_scenes data blob and its readers, and the test coverage that would actually catch its failure modes. The review is the deliverable; the quality of the reasoning inside each section is what is judged.
Learning objective: Reconstruct a durable, plan-driven pipeline's plan/run contract from measured structure in the code, then reason one change through plan ordering, run-state transitions, versioned migration, persisted-blob compatibility and test coverage — and defend the result in a scoped design review.
If the learner asks what project they are doing, answer directly from this information, in the project content language. Never say you do not know the project, and never ask them what project they want to do unless the project title and description are empty.

projectV2.title: Extend the OpenMAIC Generation Pipeline: A Defensible Design Review

milestones.title: Recon the pipeline from measured structure
milestones.debrief: That map is now the yardstick for the rest of the project — every later claim about plan position, run states, migration or blob impact has to land on it. If any hop still feels fuzzy, mark it: that is precisely where your own change will get you into trouble later.
milestones.briefing: Welcome to stage one. Open your OpenMAIC checkout and treat it as an unknown system — no shortcuts through documentation. What I want from you is a map you'd defend line by line: which modules own the plan, which own the run, how a step moves between states, who writes those transitions when a worker dies mid-step, and where the document_scenes blob and the DSL version first appear in code. Bring me paths and symbols, not summaries. If I ask 'which file?' and you answer 'the generation layer', we go back and look again. Show me your layer table when you're ready and we'll harden it together.

hints: Start at the process entry point and only descend into a module when its imports tell you it does real work — which modules own orchestration, and which merely translate data between shapes?
If two modules appear to own the same decision, find which one holds the mutable state — that one is upstream.
microtasks.title: Map the layer boundaries
microtasks.description: Produce a table of the pipeline's layers: for each row give the layer's responsibility, one representative file path, the exported symbol that crosses into the next layer, and the payload that crosses with it. Done well means every row's boundary is backed by an actual call site you can open, and no row is just a folder name with a vague responsibility.

hints: Search for where the state field is written, not where it is read — writes reveal the transitions that actually exist.
Ask what separates a step that reported failure from one that went silent: which mechanism notices, and how long does it wait?
microtasks.title: Reconstruct the run state machine
microtasks.description: Enumerate the states a run and an individual step can be in, the trigger that moves each one, the component that writes the transition, the side effect it causes, and whether the state is terminal. Add a short written account of crash recovery: what happens to a step whose owner dies, and what distinguishes a step that failed from one whose owner vanished. Done well means every transition names a writer and you can state the recovery path for a mid-step crash in concrete terms.

hints: Find the hop where the step's output stops being an in-memory value and becomes a stored field — that hop is the one your own change will have to extend.
If you cannot say what a retry of an existing step would re-execute, you do not yet understand the durability model you are about to change.
microtasks.title: Trace one existing step end to end
microtasks.description: Pick any existing generation step and write a numbered hop trace from plan construction through execution to the persisted document_scenes blob. Name every file and symbol at each hop, list the blob keys your chosen step contributes, and state what a retry of that step would re-do versus reuse. Done well means the trace reaches the persisted blob, not just the in-memory result, and the retry semantics are stated rather than assumed.

milestones.description: Build a defensible map of OpenMAIC's generation pipeline in your own checkout: entry points, the plan layer versus the run layer, the run state machine including crash recovery, and where the document_scenes blob and the DSL version actually surface in code. Every later claim in this project is checked against this map.

synthesisCheck.coreConcept: Why a durable pipeline stores intent as data — plan steps plus run state — instead of encoding it as control flow, and what resume, retry, idempotency and observability each silently depend on that choice.

milestones.completionCriteria: You're done with this stage when your map cites only paths and symbols that exist in your checkout, every claimed layer boundary has a call site you can point at, your state table names who WRITES each transition rather than who reads the state, and you can describe what happens to a single step when its worker disappears mid-execution without hedging.

milestones.title: Scope the extension you will defend
milestones.debrief: Good — you now have one bounded change instead of a wish list. The two things I'll keep testing from here: does this stay inside the seam you drew, and can you still explain the retry behaviour without hand-waving? Hold on to the out-of-scope list; it is the first thing a reviewer will attack.
milestones.briefing: Now the design starts. Pick ONE extension: a new generation step, a new agent skill, a new DSL element, or a new agent capability. Not two, not a family — one, and one you can carry through the whole project. Then place it exactly: where it sits in the plan, what must be finished before it runs, which run states it enters, which transitions it adds or changes, who writes them, and what it does on retry. Finish by writing down what you are deliberately NOT touching. I'd rather see a small change with a clean seam than an ambitious one with a foggy boundary — tell me your choice and why the alternatives lost.

hints: Name today's workaround and what it costs a real user — that is stronger evidence for a pipeline slot than any feature description.
If your extension could live as a plain library function called from an existing step, is it genuinely a new step?
microtasks.title: Commit to one extension and state the failure it removes
microtasks.description: Write a one-paragraph intent: what is impossible or painful today without your change, which concrete consumer benefits (a person, a downstream step, or an external reader of the output), and why the cheapest alternative — doing it by hand, or folding it into an existing step — is insufficient. Done well means the current workaround is described concretely, with its cost in manual steps or minutes, and the consumer is named rather than implied.

hints: Which upstream step produces your input? If none does, your work probably belongs before the pipeline starts rather than inside it.
Decide deliberately whether re-execution overwrites, skips, or reconciles — leaving it implicit is how duplicate output gets written in practice.
microtasks.title: Place it in the plan and the state machine
microtasks.description: Decide where your step sits in the plan — ordering constraints, which upstream output it consumes, whether it can run alongside other steps — and write the run-state delta: states it enters, transitions it adds or changes, who writes each one, and what happens if it is re-executed after a crash (overwrite, skip, or reconcile). Done well means the plan diagram shows explicit dependencies and every state in the delta has a named writer; a state you cannot attribute to a writer is not designed yet.

hints: Which single existing call site can carry your change with the smallest edit at the highest seam, instead of a wide refactor?
What would a reviewer call a 'while you're in there' change? List those now so you don't drift into them mid-project.
microtasks.title: Fix the blast radius
microtasks.description: List the files you will touch, the contract each edit crosses, and why the change belongs at that seam rather than a broader one. Then write an explicit out-of-scope list: the things you will be tempted to refactor but will not, each with a reason. Done well means each file has a one-line rationale, the number of touched files stays small enough to review in one sitting, and the out-of-scope reasons are substantive rather than 'later'.

milestones.description: Commit to exactly one extension — a new generation step, a new agent skill, a new DSL element, or a new agent capability — and place it precisely in the plan and the run state machine. Trim it to the smallest slice you can defend to a maintainer.
milestones.completionCriteria: You're done when one extension is named, its plan position and upstream dependencies are fixed and consistent with your stage-one map, its run-state delta lists every new or changed transition with a named writer and explicit resume/retry semantics, and your out-of-scope list gives a concrete reason (risk, later work, or genuinely unnecessary) for each deferred item. A maintainer reading your one-paragraph intent should be able to accept or reject it without asking what it covers.

milestones.title: Contract, migration and blob compatibility
milestones.debrief: This is the part of the design most likely to be accepted or rejected on, and you now have an argument rather than a hope. Keep the run walkthrough — it will become the strongest section of your review, because it is the one a reviewer cannot fake.
milestones.briefing: This is the stage that separates a sketch from a design. Three questions, in order. One: how is your change versioned, and what happens to a plan written last week — migrated on read, migrated in place, or served by a compatibility branch? Two: what does your change do to the document_scenes blob, and what do the other readers of that blob do when they meet it? Three: what happens to the run that is mid-step when your code lands — because you will not get a clean drain. Answer all three with named files, ordered steps and a stated fallback, then walk one real suspended run from its old state to its new one.

hints: Answer this before choosing a version story: would a plan written last week still validate and execute after your change?
Which is cheaper to get wrong — a plan that fails loudly on read, or a plan that silently loses a field it used to carry?
microtasks.title: Decide the version and migration policy
microtasks.description: Choose whether your change is additive or breaking for the DSL, decide how the version is recorded, and pick how persisted plans are handled: migrated eagerly, migrated lazily on read, or served by a compatibility branch. State how long older-version support lasts and what happens if the migration runs twice. Done well means the decision names the rejected alternatives with the reason each lost, the migration steps appear in execution order, and idempotency is asserted explicitly rather than assumed.

hints: Who reads this blob besides the code you are editing? Prove it by finding the read sites rather than assuming the generation code is the only consumer.
For each direction, decide: does the older side ignore your field, mis-render it, or refuse the blob? And does your new code tolerate the field being absent?
microtasks.title: Bound the document_scenes impact
microtasks.description: Show the before/after shape of the parts of the document_scenes blob your change adds, moves or removes, then name every reader of those fields — the generation code you're changing, plus any renderer, editor, exporter or diff view that consumes the blob. Build a compatibility matrix of writer version against reader version, covering blobs written before your change and readers that know nothing about your field. Done well means every cell carries a concrete verdict — works, degrades in a described way, or rejects — with no 'unknown' left standing.

hints: Do not assume a drain — design for the run that is mid-step at the moment the new code lands.
If the new worker does not recognise a step type, is the right answer to fail the run, skip the step, or hand it back to the old code path? Argue for one.
microtasks.title: Walk an in-flight run across the deploy
microtasks.description: Narrate one suspended run that spans your deploy from start state to end state: what the old worker was doing, what the new code sees when it claims the step, how an unknown or renamed step type is treated, and how lease expiry, heartbeat and the last checkpoint interact with your change. Done well means each hop names the run state and the step state at that moment, and the unknown-step case has an explicit fallback rather than 'should not happen'.

milestones.description: Design the version story for your change: whether the DSL element or version is additive or breaking, how persisted plans and in-flight runs survive the deploy, what your change does to the document_scenes data blob, and how readers that never heard of your change behave.

synthesisCheck.coreConcept: Why a persisted contract — DSL version, plan records, stored blobs — has to evolve through an explicit, idempotent migration path rather than by changing the shape in place, and how in-flight runs and older readers constrain what 'additive' is actually allowed to mean.

milestones.completionCriteria: You're done when the migration decision states what was rejected and why, the migration steps are ordered and explicitly idempotent (including what happens if they run twice), the compatibility matrix has a concrete verdict in every cell for both older blobs read by new code and newer blobs read by old readers, and your in-flight run walkthrough ends in a named run state and step state with a stated fallback for a step type the new code does not recognise.

milestones.title: Prove it with tests, then defend it
milestones.debrief: You set out to defend one bounded change to a durable pipeline, and you now have the whole chain: measured structure, plan position, run-state delta, migration, blob compatibility, test coverage and rollback. That is the shape of a real contribution to OpenMAIC, and the same reading-and-reasoning loop is what you'll use on every change you propose from here.
milestones.briefing: Last stage. A design that cannot be falsified is not finished, so we start by making something fail: take the persisted shape your change touches, build a minimal before/after fixture, and write one test that fails on the un-migrated version for the reason you predicted. Then cover the change properly — for each contract you altered, which test level catches which specific bug — and pre-mortem three ways this ships and breaks. Finally, assemble everything into the review itself. I want it to stand alone without your working notes, and I want you to end by telling me which questions you still cannot answer. That list is not a weakness; hiding it would be.

hints: Keep the fixture as small as it can be while still crossing the version boundary — one field and one version marker is usually enough.
Which test level can you actually drive here: a pure function over a plan object, or something that needs a started run? Pick accordingly.
microtasks.title: Make the migration testable — write the red test
microtasks.description: Produce a minimal before/after fixture for the persisted shape your change touches: a document_scenes blob or a plan record. Use a real one from your checkout if you can produce it; otherwise hand-write the smallest JSON that still exercises the version boundary and label it clearly as a sketch. Then write and run one test that fails against the un-migrated fixture. Done well means the failure is the one you predicted, the failure message names the missing field or behaviour, and you paste the observed output rather than describing it.

hints: For each row ask: what wrong behaviour would pass a naive test of this? If you cannot answer, the test is not pinning anything down.
For each risk, what would you see before a user reports it? If the answer is 'nothing', you have found a missing signal rather than a missing mitigation.
microtasks.title: Coverage matrix and pre-mortem
microtasks.description: For every contract your change alters, state the test level that covers it, the fixture or seed it needs, and the specific bug it would catch — including at least one test for the unknown-step path and one for a resumed run. Then list three ways this change ships and breaks in production, each with the signal you would watch and the mitigation or rollback. Done well means no row says 'increase coverage' or 'test the new step', and every risk names an observable metric, log line or queryable state plus a defined action.

hints: Read your own review as the maintainer who has to approve it on a Friday: find every place you wrote 'should work' instead of naming the file, the state and the test.
Which section would you least want to defend out loud? Start your open-questions list there.
microtasks.title: Assemble and stress the review
microtasks.description: Build the final design review from your earlier artefacts under fixed sections — Problem, Measured structure, Proposed change, Plan and run-state delta, DSL migration, document_scenes compatibility, Test coverage, Risks and rollback — then walk your proposed change once through your own stage-one map and confirm every hop resolves to a named file, a named state and a named test. Finish with the three hardest questions a hostile reviewer would ask that you cannot yet answer, and how you would resolve each. Done well means the document stands alone without your working notes, every unresolved hop is either fixed or listed as an open question, and the open questions are specific enough to be actionable.

milestones.description: Turn your change into a testable claim: one executable artefact that currently fails, a coverage matrix where every row names the bug it catches, a risk register with observability and rollback, and the assembled design review you can stand behind.
milestones.completionCriteria: You're done when your red test fails for the predicted reason with a failure message naming the missing field or behaviour, every coverage row names a concrete bug rather than a coverage target, each risk names an observable signal and a defined rollback or kill switch, and the assembled review resolves every hop of your change to a named file, a named state and a named test — with anything that does not resolve listed explicitly as an open question with a plan to close it.

projectV2.description: Design exactly one concrete extension to OpenMAIC — a new generation step, a new agent skill, a new DSL element, or a new agent capability — and produce a design review that names the files and contract boundaries it crosses, its position in the plan and the run-state transitions it adds, the DSL and persisted-plan migration path, its impact on the document_scenes data blob and its readers, and the test coverage that would actually catch its failure modes. The review is the deliverable; the quality of the reasoning inside each section is what is judged.
projectV2.languageDirective: Deliver the entire course in English, written for an experienced software engineer who reads code. Keep all identifiers, file paths, table names, API routes, package names and code symbols in their original English form (e.g. lib/server/generation/run/plan.ts, document_scenes, @openmaic/dsl) — never translate or paraphrase them. Use precise technical vocabulary without dumbing it down, and prefer concrete artefacts and measured numbers over product-level description. Where a term has a standard engineering meaning (lease, heartbeat, checkpoint, JSONB, migration), use it directly and assume familiarity.
projectV2.learningObjective: Reconstruct a durable, plan-driven pipeline's plan/run contract from measured structure in the code, then reason one change through plan ordering, run-state transitions, versioned migration, persisted-blob compatibility and test coverage — and defend the result in a scoped design review.
